overview: A monosaccharide is a single sugar unit; a disaccharide is two monosaccharides joined together.
genZNote: Monosaccharide: solo sugar. Disaccharide: sugar duo holding hands via a glycosidic bond.

aspects.label: Number of Sugar Units
aspects.valueA: One simple sugar unit; cannot be hydrolysed further.
aspects.valueB: Two monosaccharide units joined by a glycosidic bond; can be hydrolysed back into monosaccharides.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueB: Sucrose (glucose + fructose), lactose (glucose + galactose), maltose (glucose + glucose).

aspects.label: Digestion Needed?
aspects.valueA: Absorbed directly into the bloodstream without further digestion.
aspects.valueB: Must be hydrolysed by enzymes into monosaccharides before absorption.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Lactose intolerance is a classic exam link — it results from a deficiency of the enzyme lactase needed to break lactose into its monosaccharides.
overlay.memoryTrick: Mono = one. Di = two, joined and needing to be split apart before absorption.
overlay.commonMisconception: A disaccharide is not simply 'two monosaccharides mixed together' — they are covalently bonded and require an enzyme to separate.
